extracted.intended_audience: scientists, naturalists, lepidopterists, and educated readers of Nature
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidance and commentary for natural-history monographs and scientific exhibits, covering qualities of illustrations, descriptions, experimental evidence, materials, and instruments as presented in a Nature news/review piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tables and descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The tables and descriptions should be very carefully drawn up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review praises 'The tables and descriptions are very carefully drawn up' — careful, precise tabulation and descriptive text are expected for a taxonomic/monographic work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and purpose of illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrations, both coloured and uncoloured, should represent venation, legs, and other important structural characters and be worthy of high praise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include both coloured plates and line/structural figures; uncoloured figures often should show venation, legs, and other key morphological details. Avoid excessive reduction of important figures of large species (criticised when reduced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage of life-history and behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Transformations, broods, habits, flight, scent, stridulation, etc., should be fully discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A comprehensive monograph ought to treat life-history aspects (transformations, broods), behavioural notes, and special organs or actions, not just taxonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of comparative references
rubrics_metrics.description: References to the transformations of common comparative species should be included unless clearly redundant or unavailable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review notes omission of references to European species' transformations; such comparative references aid readers and should be included unless intentionally omitted (e.g., to avoid repeating widely available info) or records are lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness and accuracy of range/destribution statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographical ranges should be given completely and accurately; avoid wording that unintentionally excludes known localities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the range of Colias was incompletely given (omitting Lapland, South Africa); careful checking and inclusive phrasing are required for distributional statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlighting novel observations
rubrics_metrics.description: New and interesting observations (behaviours, biological interactions) should be recorded and emphasised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novel notes (e.g., a Lycaenide 'milking' an aphis) are of special interest and should be clearly presented and illustrated when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and detail in morphological descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Original, curious, and detailed morphological descriptions (e.g., of tentacles or larval structures) are valuable and should be included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer singled out original descriptions (tentacles of Curetis bulis) — encourage clear, novel morphological descriptions with illustrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal beyond specialist audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Works should contain material that appeals to the general naturalist as well as specialists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A monograph that 'appeals to the general naturalist, and not merely to the lepidopterist' is considered desirable; include broader-natural-history content where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental evidence and sterile technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims based on experiments (e.g., origin of organisms) should be supported by demonstrated adequacy of sterilisation, sterile handling, and prompt documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequacy of sterilisation must be shown; organisms should be removed onto sterilised slips and promptly photographed; multiple independent specimens and repeated observations strengthen claims and help rebut alternative explanations (e.g., contamination or parasitism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity and repeatability of observational evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide multiple specimens, repeated observations, and photographic documentation to support unusual or controversial biological claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes taking 'some hundreds of Otostomata' and showing about fifty specimens — demonstrating abundance in one's material and repeatability is essential for credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstration of principles via working models
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical or engineering principles should be explained and shown by means of working models and demonstrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: explanation of Brennan's mono-railway 'by means of a working model' — clear demonstration helps communicate mechanism and applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material purity and manufacturability for apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: For new material-based apparatus (iridium, rhodium), extreme purity and resultant manufacturability (malleability) and chemical/thermal properties are key merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Materials that were 'hitherto practically unworkable' become valuable when produced pure enough to make basins, tubes, flasks; note high melting point and resistance to acids as desirable properties for chemical research apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thermal and chemical robustness of laboratory glassware
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparatus (e.g., fused silica ware) should withstand rapid cooling/thermal shock and be chemically resistant (unattacked by water/acids).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Desirable properties include ability to be plunged white-hot into water without cracking, resistance to acids/water, low coefficient of expansion — these make materials valuable to science and industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument accuracy, sensitivity, and user-readout
rubrics_metrics.description: Measuring and optical instruments should demonstrate high accuracy, appropriate sensitivity, rapid operation where needed, and clear/readable output (e.g., direct wavelength readout).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: measuring machine accuracy 'greater than 1 in 200,000' and speed 'one per minute'; diffraction spectroscope with micrometer reading sine of angle to give wavelength directly; heliochronometer giving GMT and self-correcting for equation of time — design for usability and precision is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrable scientific novelty and reproducible experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Exhibits and experiments should show new effects or confirm known phenomena under controlled conditions and be reproducible and well-explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include radiometer experiments showing cessation of action in very high vacua, persistent electric oscillations for wireless telegraphy, and vacuum electroscope effects; each display should document conditions, reproducible outcomes, and explanatory context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative and provenance-backed biological displays
rubrics_metrics.description: Biological exhibits should include representative specimens, series illustrating transformations, and clear provenance (collector, locality, date) to permit scientific comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The conversazione exhibits included series showing metamorphosis (e.g., eel leptocephalus to elver), specimens from Antarctic Discovery, and casts/skins with collector attribution — such context and series enhance scientific value.
